summary:
Missouri's Save Adolescents from Experimentation (SAFE) Act, enacted in 2023 as Senate Bill 49, has been in force since 28 August 2023. It prohibits anyone under 18 from starting gender-affirming hormones or puberty blockers, allows those already in treatment to continue, and bans all transition-related surgery for minors. A state judge denied a preliminary injunction on 29 August 2023, and the statute took effect on schedule.

The same law bars MO HealthNet, the state Medicaid programme, from paying for gender-affirming care for a patient of any age, restricts treatment access in prisons, jails and correctional centres, and exposes providers who violate it to loss of their Missouri medical licence and to patient lawsuits brought up to 15 years after treatment.

Litigation began with a complaint filed 25 July 2023 in Cole County Circuit Court by Lambda Legal, the ACLU of Missouri and Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, acting for three families of transgender young people, medical providers, PFLAG National and GLMA. Following a trial in September 2024, Judge Robert Craig Carter upheld the ban on 25 November 2024 and the plaintiffs announced an appeal. The Missouri Supreme Court affirmed unanimously on 13 January 2026, quoting the 2025 U.S. Supreme Court ruling that upheld Tennessee's comparable ban. The statute sunsets in 2027, lawmakers have stated they want it made permanent, and a November 2026 ballot initiative seeks to bar such care indefinitely.

Care in custody is separately restricted. Governor Mike Kehoe signed HB 2009, effective 2 July 2026, providing that no funds shall be expended for any cross-sex hormones or gender transition surgery undertaken for the purpose of any gender transition, with no taper plan for inmates already receiving care. Missouri became the seventh state to deny gender-affirming care to incarcerated people and the second in 2026 to do so. Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina have near-identical laws, while comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia were blocked by federal courts.

Trans athletes are barred from female sports. Senate Bill 39, signed 7 June 2023, requires public and private schools through college to restrict sports participation to sex assigned at birth; the ban carries a sunset clause repealing it automatically on 28 August 2027.

Identity documents carry a surgical requirement. A change of sex on a Missouri birth certificate requires a court order with certified proof on hospital letterhead, signed by the attending physician with licence and contact details, stating that the petitioner's physical sex has been altered and the surgical changes are irreversible, under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 193.215(9). Two 2013 cases that had permitted an exception were invalidated and reversed in May 2022, leaving no route around the surgical requirement. The Department of Revenue accepted Form 5532 for changing the gender designation on a licence or ID after policy review between 2016 and 2024, then reverted to requiring surgery documentation or a court order after an unspecified incident.

Protection machinery is uneven. Missouri's hate crime statutes explicitly cover gender identity, defined as "having a self-image or identity not traditionally associated with one's gender," while state non-discrimination legislation does not address gender identity at all.
tangentialFactors:
Missouri's care ban for incarcerated people belongs to a wider state-level pattern: seven states now deny gender-affirming care to inmates, and Missouri is the second to enact such a measure in 2026. Court outcomes diverge sharply by jurisdiction, with near-identical statutes standing in Florida, Kentucky and North Carolina and comparable measures in Idaho and Georgia blocked by federal courts.

The Missouri Attorney General issued emergency orders in March and April 2023 declaring gender-affirming care experimental. The adult-care order, set to expire February 2024, would have required three years of documented intense dysphoria, at least 15 psychiatric sessions over 18 months with at least 10 with the same therapist, treatment of comorbidities, autism screening, 15-year adverse-effect tracking, annual dysphoria assessment, screening for social contagion, written consent every three months for three years and detailed compliance records. A judge temporarily blocked it and the Attorney General withdrew it in May 2023, along with the parallel youth-care orders of March and April 2023.

The direction of travel in the legislature runs toward permanence rather than expiry: the SAFE Act's 2027 sunset was a partisan concession at enactment, and both lawmakers and a November 2026 ballot initiative are now moving to remove it.

Before the 2022 reversal, two 2013 cases had allowed a birth-certificate change without the surgical certification; their invalidation closed the only documented workaround, so the current document rule is stricter in practice than the statute alone suggests.
localsOnly:
Missouri has no state law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of gender identity. The only related instrument is a 2010 executive order providing sexual-orientation protections for government employees; a Senate-passed bill banning sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, housing and public accommodations passed 19-11 in 2013 and died when the House adjourned without considering it.

The state operates a tipline for anonymous reporting of suspected violations of the care ban and for general complaints about a "gender transition intervention."

Kansas City declared itself a sanctuary city for transgender individuals and rights in May 2023, and Columbia voted in February 2024 to include LGBT protections in its sanctuary ordinance.

Missouri has no law limiting adoption on the basis of LGBT status under Mo. Ann. Stat. § 453.010, with no explicit prohibition on same-sex or second-parent adoption. Domestic partnership registries in Clayton, Columbia, Jackson County, Kansas City, Olivette, St Louis and University City grant certain benefits within their borders to both opposite- and same-sex couples.

In August 2021, SB53 reformed the state's 1980s-era HIV criminalisation laws, reducing the offence from a felony to a misdemeanor.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources date the denial of the preliminary injunction against the SAFE Act differently: one report places it on 29 August 2023, another in August 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

Whether HB 2009's funding bar reaches pre-trial detainees as well as sentenced prisoners is not stated in the sources.

The Department of Revenue's reversal of its Form 5532 gender-marker policy is attributed only to an "unspecified incident"; no date, internal guidance or legal challenge to the reverted policy is documented, and whether the current requirement has been litigated is unresolved.

The sources contain no dated incident of violence against a trans person in Missouri, with an outcome, so no such incident can be stated. They also provide no Missouri-specific figure for trans people held in state custody.

Whether the SAFE Act's 2027 sunset will be extended by legislation and what the November 2026 ballot initiative yields are unresolved.

No Missouri-specific rule governing airport screening or entry inspection of trans travellers appears in the sources; any such exposure would arise under federal rather than state authority.
